result.summary: Pausanias describes the territory of Orchomenus in Arcadia, beginning with the temple of Hymnian Artemis and her strictly separated priests. He then describes the old and new town, its sights, and the roads and landmarks leading toward Caphya, Stymphelus and Pheneus.

scenes.title: Temple of Hymnian Artemis
scenes.summary: The temple of Hymnian Artemis stands on the mountain slope. Its priestess and priest live apart and keep strict purity, which Pausanias compares to the Ephesian priests.

scenes.title: Orchomenus and its sights
scenes.summary: The old town stood on a hill; the present town lies within the old walls. Pausanias lists its well, temples, the cedar-tree Artemis, unknown war tombs and the plain.

scenes.title: Roads toward Caphya and Pheneus
scenes.summary: Pausanias traces roads from Orchomenus past the tomb of Aristocrates, the Teneae wells and Amilus, then toward Pheneus through a ravine to Caryae.

alias_notes.explanation: Ephesian Artemis's priests are called Histiatores by themselves but Essenes by the citizens.
Variant form of the goddess's cult title.

analysis.text: The passage shows Pausanias' periegetic method: cult practice, ruins and roads are recorded together as a guided walk through Arcadia.
The priests' lifelong separation reflects Greek ideas of ritual purity, which Pausanias compares with the yearly practice at Ephesus.

language_notes.text: Mantineans are the people of Mantinea, a neighbouring Arcadian city, who shared the cult.
Histiatores and Essenes are cult titles for attendants of Ephesian Artemis; "Essenes" here is unrelated to the Jewish sect of that name.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180–200 metres.
Pausanias refers to a known story that Aristocrates, an Arcadian king, violated the priestess; he tells it elsewhere, so only the crime is noted here.
"Projects" means juts out; the Caphyatic rock is a cliff overhanging the road.

context_notes.text: Ephesus in Asia Minor housed the great temple of Artemis; its priests also practised periods of ritual purity.
Poseidon and Aphrodite had temples across Arcadia, despite its inland setting.
Artemis was worshipped under local titles; a cult image hung in a living tree reflects very old tree-worship.

literary_notes.text: The priests' lifelong separation portrays the cult as austere and sets a tone of reverent strictness.
The short sentence set against the old hilltop town marks the town's decline and shift of site.
The tombs honour fallen men, yet their enemy and even their cause are forgotten, undercutting the monuments' purpose.
